diminutive

/dih-MIN-yuh-tiv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Diminutive means remarkably or extremely small in size.

Next to the towering draft horses, the diminutive pony at the county fair looked like a plush toy that had wandered out of the gift shop.

Example

The harbor pilot climbed aboard the diminutive tugboat, a vessel dwarfed by the container ship it had come to guide. Onlookers on the pier marveled that a boat so strikingly small could steer a giant hundreds of times its weight safely into port.

The tugboat's strikingly small size next to the enormous container ship is exactly what diminutive describes: remarkable smallness that you notice at a glance.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tiny: Tiny simply means extremely small, and it is the plain, everyday word: a tiny crumb, a tiny apartment. Diminutive adds a note of surprise or affection at how remarkably small something is for its kind, the way a diminutive pony stands out beside full-sized horses.

minuscule: Minuscule means so small it is hard to notice at all: a minuscule typo, a minuscule speck of dust. Diminutive things are strikingly small but still plainly visible; their smallness is the first thing you see, not something you strain to find.

miniature: Miniature means made as a much smaller copy of something larger, like dollhouse furniture or a model train. A miniature is small on purpose, by design. Diminutive describes a real thing that happens to be remarkably small for its kind, not a scaled-down replica.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

enormous: extremely large

towering: impressively tall or large

Where it sits · how far below normal size it falls — small → diminutive → microscopic

small vs. diminutive: Something small is simply below average size, while something diminutive is so remarkably small that its size is the first thing you notice.

microscopic vs. diminutive: A diminutive object is strikingly tiny but still easy to see, whereas a microscopic one is too small to see without special equipment.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — diminut

Root — diminut: from Latin deminuere, to lessen or make smaller

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: adjective-forming ending, having the quality of

Put it together

Put it together: Diminutive comes from Latin deminuere, 'to lessen or make smaller.' The root diminut- means 'lessened,' and the suffix -ive turns it into an adjective: something diminutive looks as if it has been shrunk down from normal size. The same Latin root gives us diminish, 'to make or become smaller.'

Use the root in a new word: diminish

Use the root in a new word: diminish: As the drought dragged on, the reservoir continued to diminish week by week, and the town posted new watering restrictions every Monday.

Word Choice

formal, often admiring or affectionate

Diminutive describes physical size and often carries a tone of surprise or affection, as in 'the diminutive gymnast' or 'a diminutive cottage.' In grammar, a diminutive is also a word form that signals smallness, such as duckling from duck. Keep it for the visible size of things and creatures, not for small amounts or quantities.
